passages.P4: Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa[2][3][4][5] and the sixth most populous in the world.[6][7] Nigeria is also one of the most densely populated countries in Africa, with approximately 237 million people as of 2025[8] in an area of 923,768 km2 (356,669 sq mi).[9][10]
passages.P5: 54.3% of Nigerians are urban dwellers, with the annual rate of urbanisation being estimated at 3.92%.[2][a] Nigeria is home to 250 ethnic groups speaking over 500 languages[2] and the variety of customs and traditions among them gives the country great cultural diversity. The three largest ethnic groups, namely the Hausas, Yorubas, and Igbos constitute more than 60% of the population.[2][11][12][13] The Ijaw, Efik, Ibibio, Annang, Ogoni, Tiv, Urhobo-Isoko, Edo, and Itsekiri are some of the other sizeable ethnic groups.[14] Over 1.2 million people living in Nigeria (0.5% of its total population, or 1 in every 200 people living in Nigeria) are from a continent other than Africa. In particular, 100,000 people are from the United States,[15] 75,000 are from Lebanon,[16] 60,000 are from China,[17] and 16,000 are from the United Kingdom.[18]
passages.P6: Nigeria has a young population overall, with 42.54% of inhabitants between the ages of 0–14.[2][19] There is also a very high dependency ratio at 88.2 dependents per 100 non-dependents.[2] The three main religious groups are Muslims (estimated to be 53.5% of the total population), Christians (estimated at 45.9%), and adherents of indigenous religions (estimated at 0.6%).[20] The predominantly Christian Igbo are found in the south-east.[21] Roman Catholicism is the largest Christian denomination in Igboland,[22][23][24] but Anglicanism is also strong, as are Pentecostalism and other Evangelical denominations.
passages.P7: Persons of different ethnic backgrounds most commonly communicate in English, although knowledge of two or more Nigerian languages is widespread. Hausa, Igbo, and Yoruba are the most widely used Nigerian languages. Nigerian Pidgin is used widely as an unofficial medium of communication, especially in the Nigerian cities of Warri, Sapele, Ughelli, Benin, and Port Harcourt.[25]
